intro: Istanbul is the only city in the world that was capital to two empires without ever changing location: Constantinople and Istanbul tread on each other at every corner of Sultanahmet. You'll count heads that are no longer there, decode a Viking runic graffito carved by a mercenary of the Byzantine imperial guard, and track down a Christian eagle hiding above an Ottoman gate. It's just over 3 km all told, with one gentle climb up toward the Grand Bazaar and the same easy walk back down.
puntoPartida: Sultanahmet Square, on the landscaped ground between Hagia Sophia (Ayasofya) and the Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Camii)

paradas.titulo: The Four Minarets That Don't Match
paradas.llegada: Standing in Sultanahmet Square facing Hagia Sophia, step back until you can see the whole building and all four of its minarets, one at each corner.
paradas.enigma: Hagia Sophia was a Christian cathedral for almost a thousand years before becoming a mosque in 1453: its four minarets are a later Ottoman addition, built at different times by different sultans. Compare all four carefully — three match each other in colour and material, but the fourth clearly doesn't fit. What colour is the minaret that doesn't match the other three?
pistas: Look at the material, not just the shape — three of the minarets are pale stone.
The odd one out is the oldest of the four, dating from the late 15th century.
It's the red-brick minaret, on the southeast corner — very different from the white of the other three.
paradas.historia: Hagia Sophia's first minaret, made of wood, hasn't survived: Mehmed II had it built the moment he turned the cathedral into a mosque, in 1453. The one you see today on the southeast corner, built in brick, dates from somewhat later, the end of the 15th century. The other three — slender, in pale limestone — were added during the 16th century; two of them are the work of the great Ottoman architect Mimar Sinan, the same man who reinforced the whole building against the earthquakes that already shook the city.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Hagia Sophia; hagiasophia.com — Hagia Sophia Minarets

paradas.titulo: The Viking Who Signed the Balustrade
paradas.llegada: This stop is on Hagia Sophia's upper gallery, reachable only by paying for the 'visiting area' ticket (compulsory for tourists since 2024, around 25 EUR). If you're not going in, just read the story and move on to stop 3. If you do go in, climb to the south gallery and look for a marble balustrade beside one of the windows.
paradas.enigma: On one of that balustrade's marble slabs there are some carved vertical strokes that look like simple scratches — but they're Norse runes: a Viking guard carved them there over a thousand years ago, probably bored during a long ceremony, while serving in the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard. Scholars have managed to read a Scandinavian first name among those strokes, almost certainly belonging to whoever carved them. What Norse name has been identified in this inscription?
pistas: It's a Scandinavian man's name, not a saint or a Byzantine emperor.
It starts with 'Hal-' and means roughly 'half-Dane'.
The name carved here is Halvdan (also spelled Halfdan).
paradas.historia: The Varangian Guard was the elite corps of the Byzantine army, made up of Scandinavian and, later, Anglo-Saxon mercenaries who served as the emperor's personal bodyguard from the 10th century onward. This graffito, identified in 1964, is one of two known runic inscriptions in Hagia Sophia. Carving your own name into stone, far from home, isn't so different from what people do today with a marker pen at any monument — except Halvdan used runes, and his have been here for over a thousand years.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Runic inscriptions in Hagia Sophia; hagia-sophia.istanbul — Viking Graffiti (Varangian Guard)

paradas.titulo: The Six Towers That Alarmed Mecca
paradas.llegada: Turn your back on Hagia Sophia: the Blue Mosque stands in front of you, its minarets cutting into the sky. Count them all, including the thinner, more distant ones — no need to go inside.
paradas.enigma: Almost every Ottoman imperial mosque has four minarets at most; some have only one or two. When Sultan Ahmed I finished this mosque in 1616, it caused an uproar across the Islamic world, because only one other building had as many minarets as this one: the Great Mosque of Mecca, Islam's holiest site. How many minarets does the Blue Mosque have?
pistas: Four stand at the corners of the main building, and two smaller ones at the corners of the courtyard.
It's the same number the Great Mosque of Mecca had at the time — hence the uproar.
There are 6 minarets in total.
paradas.historia: Legend says the sultan asked for 'altın' (golden) minarets and the architect, Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, misheard it as 'altı' (six) — a mix-up too neat to be true, though guides keep repeating it. The documented version is less fun: Ahmed I, a young sultan who hadn't yet won any major war, wanted a mosque to match his ambition, and matching Mecca's minaret count was read as an affront. The dispute was settled by adding a seventh minaret to the mosque in Mecca, letting Istanbul keep its six.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Sultan Ahmed Mosque; traveltomorrow.com — The story behind the six minarets

paradas.titulo: The Pharaoh Who Ended Up in a Hippodrome
paradas.llegada: Walk to the long open square west of the Blue Mosque: this is the old Hippodrome of Constantinople, today a free public square. At one end stands an obelisk of reddish stone on a carved white marble pedestal.
paradas.enigma: The obelisk itself is genuinely Egyptian, carved over 3,000 years ago for the Pharaoh Thutmose III, and originally stood at the temple of Karnak. The pedestal's reliefs, by contrast, are Byzantine, from when Emperor Theodosius brought the obelisk here in the year 390. On one of the pedestal's four faces, carved figures watch something from a raised box, their hands lifted. What are the emperor and his court watching from that box?
pistas: You're standing, right now, on the very track where it happened — this square was the hippodrome.
It's a spectator sport, hugely popular in Constantinople, with vehicles pulled by horses.
The relief shows the emperor presiding over chariot races from the hippodrome's imperial box.
paradas.historia: Moving this obelisk from Egypt was a feat of logistics: it weighs around 200 tonnes, and it travelled down the Nile and then by sea to Constantinople, where it took years before it could be raised again. It broke during transport or installation, so today it stands about 18.5 metres tall — considerably less than the original, which was closer to 30. The hieroglyphs are still Thutmose III's, from the 15th century BC; the pedestal beneath it, on the other hand, was carved specifically in the 4th century for the occasion, with Greek and Latin inscriptions boasting of the feat of raising it again.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Obelisk of Theodosius; thebyzantinelegacy.com — Obelisk of Theodosius

paradas.llegada: Keep walking along the same Hippodrome square a little further, to a twisted bronze column, much lower and darker than the obelisk: it's the intertwined bodies of three serpents.
paradas.enigma: This column was cast from the bronze weapons the Greeks stripped from the defeated Persian army at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BC, and it stood for more than 800 years at the sanctuary of Delphi before Constantine brought it here. It originally ended in three serpent heads holding up a golden bowl. Look closely at the top of the column, where those heads should be. How many are still in place today?
pistas: You don't need to strain your eyes — just check whether anything head-shaped is up there at all.
All three vanished centuries ago; one fragment survives, but not here — it's in a museum.
None remain (0): all three were lost, the last one around 1700.
paradas.historia: The three serpent heads survived the journey from Delphi, the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and over a thousand years of Byzantine and Ottoman history — only to be lost in the modern era, probably to vandalism, sometime between the late 16th century and 1700. Only the fragment of one upper jaw survives, now on display in the Istanbul Archaeological Museums, less than a kilometre from here. The whole column stood about 8 metres tall with its heads; today, headless, it's just over 5.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Serpent Column; Istanbul Archaeological Museums

paradas.titulo: The Medusas Nobody Wanted to Face
paradas.llegada: This stop is inside the Basilica Cistern (Yerebatan Sarnıcı), an underground Byzantine reservoir a few steps from Hagia Sophia, with a compulsory paid entrance — there's no way to see it from outside. If you're not going in, just read the story and move on to stop 7. If you do go in, look in the northwest corner of the cistern, at the back, for two columns whose base isn't a plain stone block but a woman's face with snakes for hair.
paradas.enigma: These are two heads of Medusa, probably Roman and already ancient by the time Justinian's engineers reused them here in 532, salvaging stone from some earlier monument now lost to history. Neither one is placed facing forward normally: one is completely inverted, upside down. The other isn't inverted, but it isn't upright either. How is the second Medusa head positioned?
pistas: Look first at the upside-down one, just to rule it out — you're after the other one.
It's neither upright nor inverted — it's turned roughly 90 degrees from normal.
The second Medusa head is lying on its side.
paradas.historia: Nobody knows for certain why they were placed this way. One legend claims it was deliberate, to cancel out the power of Medusa's gaze — which in myth turned anyone who met her eyes to stone — without destroying sculptures that were still valuable. The less poetic explanation, favoured by much of current archaeology, is simpler: the Byzantine stonemasons just needed two blocks of exactly the right height to level these two columns, and the Medusa heads, already recycled from another building, happened to fit perfectly placed this way.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Basilica Cistern; yerebatan.com — Medusa Heads

paradas.titulo: The Eagle That Outlived the Empire That Carved It
paradas.llegada: Head northwest, up Yerebatan Caddesi and across the Divan Yolu avenue, to the Grand Bazaar (Kapalıçarşı) — about 15-20 minutes on foot, free to enter. Go in through the Nuruosmaniye Gate and ask for the İç Bedesten, the bazaar's oldest vaulted hall, today home to jewellers and antique dealers. On its east side, above the jewellers' gate (Kuyumcular Kapısı), look for a grey stone relief, far more worn than the gate around it.
paradas.enigma: The Grand Bazaar was built on the orders of Mehmed the Conqueror, finished around 1461 — but this particular relief is Byzantine, in a style that predates the Ottoman conquest of the city, and shows a bird with its wings spread. The Ottoman builders may have reused it from a demolished Byzantine building, or they may have placed it there on purpose, as a gesture toward the city's newly conquered Christian residents. Look closely: how many heads does the bird in the relief have?
pistas: It's no ordinary eagle — look carefully at the top, where you'd expect to find a single head.
It's the most widely repeated heraldic symbol of the whole Byzantine Empire.
It has 2 heads: it's a double-headed Byzantine eagle.
paradas.historia: This relief is sometimes used as proof that part of the building is Byzantine, but analysis of the brickwork shows the structure around it is almost entirely Ottoman, built after 1453. It's most likely a reused piece, one among thousands of fragments of old Constantinople that the Ottomans recycled while building the new Istanbul, just as they did with columns, capitals, and marble blocks across the city. The bazaar is closed on Sundays: if you're doing this route that day, you'll have to settle for seeing it from outside, through the gates' iron grilles.
paradas.fuente: kulturenvanteri.com — Kapalıçarşı; Wikipedia — Grand Bazaar, Istanbul

paradas.titulo: The Column That Was the Centre of the World
paradas.llegada: Leave the Grand Bazaar the way you came in and head back toward Sultanahmet along Divan Yolu avenue. Just before you reach the square again, level with the Basilica Cistern, look to your right for a short, solitary stone column in a small landscaped patch beside the road.
paradas.enigma: This is what remains of the Milion: a monument that, around the year 330, when Constantine founded his new capital here, marked the exact point from which every distance in the Byzantine Empire was measured — Constantinople's answer to Rome's Golden Milestone. It once consisted of several arches and columns, decorated with statues of Constantine and his mother, Helena. Of all that, how many columns are still standing here today, in plain sight?
pistas: Don't expect a grand monument — it's far smaller and plainer than you'd think.
The rest of the Milion was lost or recycled as building material centuries ago.
A single column remains (1), rebuilt from original fragments.
paradas.historia: From this point, in theory, distances were measured to every major city of the Byzantine Empire: Constantinople as the zero kilometre of the known world. The whole route you've just walked — from the minarets that don't match to the recycled eagle at the Grand Bazaar — has been uncovering incomplete monuments all along: a lone Viking signature, a headless serpent, a Byzantine eagle that outlived the gate it sits on. The Milion, reduced to this single column, may be the perfect summary of the two cities — Constantinople and Istanbul — you've spent the morning walking through at once.
paradas.fuente: Wikipedia — Milion; istanbul-tourist-information.com — Million Stone (Milyon Taşı)

final.titulo: You've Walked Through Two Empires at Once
final.texto: From a minaret that doesn't match its neighbours to a single column that was once the centre of the known world, you've covered just over 3 km over a hippodrome that no longer exists, the signature of a Viking mercenary carved into marble, and a Byzantine eagle that outlived the conquest that should have erased it. Constantinople and Istanbul have trodden on each other at every stop, without either one ever fully winning out. Next time someone asks you the name of this city, both answers will still be correct.
